item.title: US stocks have continued their declines today. What next from a technical perspective?
item.description:
In yesterday’s video, I looked at three major US stock indices. Each offered a different view of the market—and a different technical story:

  • S&P 500: The broadest sector representation of the three.

  • Nasdaq Composite: A broader collection of Nasdaq-listed companies, with a heavy technology weighting.

  • Nasdaq 100: A more concentrated index of 100 of the largest nonfinancial companies listed on Nasdaq, with significant technology exposure.

At the time, the S&P was trying to hold support at its 100-hour moving average. The Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 were trading between their 100- and 200-hour moving averages, giving sellers a modest short-term advantage.

By the close, that advantage had grown. Both Nasdaq indices finished below their 200-hour moving averages. Today, the selling has continued, bringing the next technical levels into play.

Where do the buyers need to make a stand?

  • S&P 500 — 200-hour moving average at 7,706.38: The index has now broken below that level. Stay below, and the sellers retain control of the short-term bias. Buyers need to reclaim the moving average and hold above it to begin repairing the technical damage. The

  • Nasdaq Composite — 100-day moving average at 26,289: The index gapped below its rising trendline and the 38.2% retracement at 26,463, but found support buyers just ahead of its rising 100-day moving average. That gives buyers a level to lean against and some hope. Hold above it, and a recovery toward 26,463 becomes the next test. Break below it and stay below, and another layer of support gives way.

  • Nasdaq 100 — 100-day moving average at 29,626.09: The index has already broken below this longer-term barometer and remains below it. Buyers need to reclaim that moving average and then the broken trendline near 29,700. Until those levels are recovered and held, sellers remain in control.

The trading lesson: Finding support is only the first step

The Nasdaq Composite attracted buyers near its 100-day moving average. That is a starting point, but it does not confirm that the decline is over. Buyers still need to push the price back above broken technical levels to show they are taking back control.

The same principle applies to the S&P and Nasdaq 100. Once support breaks, that level becomes a potential ceiling on a rebound. A recovery that stalls against former support gives sellers another opportunity to lean against a defined level.

Buyers need to hold support, reclaim broken levels, and keep the recovery going. Until then, the pressure remains to the downside.

In the video above, I walk through those technical levels in more detail and outline the next downside targets if the selling continues.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: AUDUSD sellers take control as economic data push the pair down over 1%. What levels matter next?
item.description:
Australia’s September jobs report was weaker than expected, giving the RBA more room to remain patient. For the AUDUSD, the report helped push the price lower. The technical breaks that followed have given sellers more control.

In the video, I look at those breaks, the levels sellers need to stay below, and the next downside targets.

Employment falls, but the details are mixed

The key seasonally adjusted figures showed:

  • Employment fell 39,300, compared with expectations for a 20,000 increase.

  • August’s gain was revised lower to 29,300 from 39,500.

  • Unemployment was 4.7%, above the 4.6% expected. August was revised to 4.7%, leaving September unchanged at the rounded level.

  • Full-time employment rose 34,400, but part-time employment fell 73,700.

  • Participation slipped to 66.8% from 67.0%.

  • Underemployment increased to 6.3% from 6.2%.

  • Hours worked edged up 0.1%.

  • The employment-to-population ratio fell 0.3 percentage points to 63.6%.

The participation decline deserves attention. With fewer people working or actively looking for work, the unemployment rate did not fully reflect the weakness in employment. The lower employment-to-population ratio reinforced that softer picture.

There were offsets. Full-time jobs increased, and hours worked edged higher. The smoother trend figures also showed employment rising 15,700, with unemployment holding at 4.6%.

My read? The report gives the RBA more room to pause, but the details are mixed enough that one weak headline does not settle the policy outlook.

Broken support gives sellers more control

For traders, the economic report provides the catalyst. The technical levels help define the bias and risk.

The move below the 0.69620–0.69778 swing area increased the bearish bias. The subsequent break below another swing area at 0.69056–0.69205 gave sellers another victory. That move was helped by the stronger PPI and retail sales report.  

That lower area is now the nearby risk-defining zone.

Stay below 0.69056–0.69205, and sellers remain in control. Move back into the area, and traders need to be alert to fading downside momentum. Get above 0.69205 and stay above, and the buyers would have a victory of their own.

A recovery would then shift attention toward the broken 38.2% retracement at 0.6950. Buyers would need to reclaim that level to improve the technical picture further.

A technical floor and the midpoint are the next targets

On the downside, the next key support zone comes between 0.68321 and 0.68632.

Within that area sits the 50% midpoint of the move higher from the November 21, 2025 low, at 0.68488.

The combination of the prior floor and the midpoint makes this an important area to watch. Sellers would first need to break below the upper boundary at 0.68632 to open the door toward the midpoint, followed by the lower boundary at 0.68321.

The trading lesson: define what would change your view

A bearish headline can push a currency lower. Sustaining that move requires sellers to defend broken support and push through the next downside targets.

The sellers have taken control. Their job now is to keep the price below the broken swing area and build on that advantage.

Can they keep the momentum going toward 0.68488? Stay below resistance, and that remains the next objective. Reclaim the broken levels, and the bearish picture starts to change.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US August business inventories +0.4% vs +0.4% expected
item.description:
• Prior was +0.8%
  • Retail inventories ex-autos vs +0.8% prior

For background, the US business inventories report, formally the Manufacturing and Trade Inventories and Sales release, is published monthly by the Census Bureau about six weeks after the reference month ends. It combines inventory and sales data from three sectors: manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers. Together they cover the bulk of goods held in the US economy.

By the time the report is released, much of it is already known. Manufacturing inventories come out earlier in the factory orders report. Advance estimates for wholesale and retail inventories arrive in the Advance Economic Indicators release roughly four weeks after month end. Business inventories completes the picture, adding the final retail figures and the combined total, which is why it rarely moves markets.

The key figures are the monthly change in total inventories and the inventory-to-sales ratio, which measures how many months it would take to sell existing stock at the current pace of sales. A rising ratio can signal weakening demand or deliberate stockpiling. A falling ratio suggests lean shelves and the potential need to restock.

The report’s main value is for GDP tracking. Changes in private inventories are one of the most volatile components of quarterly growth and can swing the headline number by a percentage point or more. Economists use the monthly data, particularly retail inventories excluding autos, to refine their GDP estimates. The figures are in nominal dollars, so periods of rapid goods inflation can inflate inventory values without any change in physical stock.

Inventory swings have taken on added importance in recent years as companies front-ran tariffs, rebuilt supply chains and adjusted to shifting trade policy, creating sharp distortions in the quarterly GDP figures.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The party continues until the money runs out. Four things have reversed bonds
item.description:
The bond market is calling time out on the AI spending spree.

For a time, no valuations were too high and no spending plans unrealistic. Now it looks like we've arrived at the reckoning as yields on bonds from CoreWeave blow out to 15%.

I have written all year about the unbelievable spending commitments on AI and data centers. It rivals spending on WW2 and is -- by far-- the greatest commitment of private capital to anything. One of the problems is a timing mismatch as the insane demand for chips and power doesn't always aling with the supply chain. That risks big slips in when data centers will come online (and be powered) compared to when the bills come due.

In addition, the rush for borrowing for these projects is competing with the US government, which continues to run deficits at 6% of GDP in good times, flooding the bond market with supply. Moreover, the US trade war is making foreign central banks turn away from the Treasury market and look to alternatives. Finally, the jump in inflation has caused the market to demand higher compensation for all bonds, making the cost of financing all this spending higher.

Of course, none of that is new.

Four things stand out for me:

1. Gavin Baker saying that the spending commitments aren't real

Baker is an AI uber-bull and he's nearly Cathie Wood levels of ridicule as he talks about SpaceX mining asteroids. At the same time, he wrote on the weekend that.

"No one - and I mean literally no one in the AI supply chain - takes the ridiculous $1 trillion of unfunded spending “commitments” from OpenAI and Anthropic even vaguely seriously.... If they could get out of the contracts they signed with OpenAI and Anthropic, they would as open-weight inference is more profitable for them than the below market prices currently being paid by OpenAI and Anthropic."

That's a big sign that much of the spending isn't going to happen and that OpenAI and Anthropic don't really have partners. Moreover, token prices have been falling rapidly lately.

2. CoreWeave, Nebius and Oracle bonds blowing out

This one speaks for itself. The bond market is the smartest market out there and they are calling bulls**t on the ability of neoclouds to make enough money to pay back the huge investments. 

3. Anthropic's numbers

Those were out late yesterday (and maybe leaked out sooner). The company disclosed $16.8 billion in Q3 revenue, which is a jump of 45% q/q but not enough to satisfy the market that it's worth $2 trillion in the upcoming IPO. There is some major fear that the IPO could mark the top.

4. How the Treasury market has reacted this week

The market reaction is often as telling as the news itself. We got hot CPI and PPI numbers in the past two days, yet we saw a big reversal in yields yesterday that's continuing today. US 10-year yields are down to 5.06% from a high of 5.34% earlier this month.

The takeaway there is that despite high inflation, there is a growing demand for safety because the AI trade could be unwinding.  It looks like The Economist called the top.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US initial jobless claim 199K vs 200K estimate
item.description:
• Initial jobless claims: 199,000, up 1,000. Prior revised to 198,000 from 197,000.

  • Initial claims four-week average: 198,500, up 250. Prior revised to 198,250 from 198,000.

  • Continuing claims: 1,710,000 for the week ending October 3, down 4,000. Prior revised to 1,714,000 from 1,716,000.

  • Continuing claims four-week average: 1,708,750, down 1,750. Prior revised to 1,710,500 from 1,711,000.

  • Insured unemployment rate: 1.1%, unchanged.

US initial jobless claims increased modestly to 199,000 in the week ending October 10, according to the Labor Department. The prior week was revised higher by 1,000, but new filings remained below the 200,000 level. Continuing claims edged lower, leaving the overall picture little changed.

The jump in unadjusted claims needs some perspective. Actual filings increased 19,456, or 11.4%, but seasonal factors had anticipated an 11.0% increase. In other words, most of that rise was expected for this time of year. Unadjusted initial claims were also below the 210,777 recorded in the comparable week last year.

Quick analysis: There is little here to suggest layoffs are picking up meaningfully. Initial claims remain low, while both continuing claims and their four-week average moved lower. That gives the Fed little additional reason to ease based on layoffs alone. A resilient labor market would normally support the dollar and yields, although these small weekly changes offer limited fresh direction. The caveat? Low layoffs do not necessarily mean strong hiring.

What this report measures: Initial claims count new applications for unemployment insurance and provide a timely signal of layoffs. Continuing claims track people receiving benefits after their initial filing, with a one-week reporting lag. The headline figures are seasonally adjusted, subject to revision, and best assessed alongside their four-week averages to smooth weekly volatility.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Canada August manufacturing sales +1.5% vs +1.1% expected
item.description:
• Prior was -0.4% (revised to -0.3%)
  • Wholesale trade -1.6% vs -1.5% expected
  • Prior trade +0.3% (revised to +0.4%)

Statistics Canada publishes two monthly reports that track activity in the goods-producing side of the economy: the Monthly Survey of Manufacturing and the Monthly Wholesale Trade Survey. Both arrive first as advance “flash” estimates, roughly three weeks after the reference month ends. Full releases follow a few weeks later with detailed industry and provincial breakdowns.

Manufacturing sales measure the value of goods shipped by Canadian factories. Key industries include petroleum and coal products, food, transportation equipment, primary metals and chemicals. Because the headline is reported in current dollars, swings in commodity prices can distort the picture, particularly through refined petroleum and metals. Markets and economists pay close attention to the constant-dollar, or volume, figure, which strips out price effects and offers a cleaner read on real output. The report also includes inventories, new orders and unfilled orders, giving a sense of where production is headed.

Wholesale trade measures sales by businesses that buy goods and resell them to retailers, other businesses and institutions. It covers sectors such as food and beverages, motor vehicles and parts, machinery and equipment, building materials and personal and household goods. Like manufacturing, it’s watched in both nominal and volume terms, alongside inventories and the inventory-to-sales ratio.

Neither report usually moves the Canadian dollar on its own, but both feed directly into monthly GDP estimates, helping economists refine growth forecasts and the Bank of Canada’s outlook. With the United States the dominant destination for Canadian goods, the data have taken on added importance as a real-time gauge of how trade policy and tariffs are hitting factories and distributors.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US retails sales for September 0.8% MoM vs 0.3% estimate. Prior month 1.3%
item.description:
• Prior 1.3%

Details

  • Retail sales MoM: +0.8% vs +0.3% expected. Prior revised to +1.2% from +1.1%.

  • Retail sales excluding autos MoM: +0.9% vs +0.5% expected. Prior revised to +1.4% from +1.3%.

  • Retail sales excluding gasoline and autos MoM: +0.2%. Prior revised to +1.2% from +1.1%.

  • Retail control group MoM: +0.1% vs +0.3% expected. Prior revised to +1.4% from +1.2%.

US retail sales were stronger than expected in September, rising 0.8% compared with the 0.3% estimate. Sales excluding autos also comfortably beat expectations, while upward revisions added to the strength of the prior month.

However, the details take some shine off the headline. Sales excluding gasoline and autos rose a more modest 0.2%. The control group, which feeds into estimates of goods consumption in gross domestic product, increased just 0.1%, missing the 0.3% estimate. That follows an upwardly revised 1.4% gain in August (from 1.2%).

Quick analysis: A strong headline, but a more mixed report underneath. The consumer continues to spend, although the softer control group points to slower momentum in the categories most relevant to the consumption calculation. Retail sales measure dollars spent, so higher prices can also lift the total without consumers buying more goods. The headline strength could support the dollar and Treasury yields and give the Fed less reason to ease, but the control-group miss tempers that message.

More Details

The biggest observation is how much gasoline contributed to the headline increase.

  • Gasoline stations accounted for 71% of September’s dollar increase. Total sales rose $5.70 billion, with gasoline station sales contributing $4.07 billion. Gas station sales jumped 6.4% for the month and 28.1% from a year ago.

  • Take out gasoline, and the report becomes more modest. Overall sales increased 0.8%, but sales excluding gasoline rose just 0.2%. Excluding both autos and gasoline, sales increased 0.3%. Spending is still growing, but the headline overstates the strength across other categories.

  • Restaurants were another bright spot. Food services and drinking places increased 1.1%, following August’s roughly 1.4% gain. Restaurants contributed another $967 million to September’s increase. Together, gasoline stations and restaurants accounted for about 88% of the total dollar gain.

  • The gains were mixed across discretionary categories. Furniture sales increased 1.3% and electronics rose 0.6%. However, clothing was essentially unchanged, general merchandise edged lower, sporting goods/hobby/book stores fell 0.5%, and miscellaneous retailers declined 3.0%. Consumers are spending, but the strength is uneven.

  • Autos were a modest contributor. Motor vehicle and parts dealer sales rose just 0.2%. That explains why sales excluding autos increased 0.9%, slightly faster than the headline.

  • Nonstore retailers continued to grow, but September’s pace slowed. Sales increased 0.3%, following approximately 2.0% in August. They remained 8.1% above a year earlier.

The important distinction is that seasonally adjusted does not mean inflation adjusted. These figures measure dollars spent. The gasoline increase alone does not tell us whether consumers bought more fuel or paid more per gallon.

My takeaway: The consumer is still spending, but this is less of a broad spending surge than the headline suggests. Gasoline did most of the heavy lifting, restaurants added support, and the remaining categories were mixed.

What this report measures:The Census Bureau’s retail sales report tracks monthly spending at retailers and food services businesses. Figures are adjusted for seasonal patterns but not inflation and are subject to revision. The control group excludes autos, gasoline, building materials and food services, helping economists estimate goods consumption within gross domestic product (GDP).

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

Manufacturing activity in the region continued to expand overall. The survey’s indicators for general activity, new orders, and shipments all declined but remained positive this month. item.title: US October Empire Manufacturing index +25.50 vs +10.25 expected
item.description:
• Prior was +7.60

Manufacturing activity in New York State expanded in October, with the Empire State Manufacturing Survey’s general business conditions index climbing 18 points to 25.5, its highest reading since December 2021.

The stronger headline reading was supported by a sharp increase in new orders and a solid rise in shipments, pointing to improving business activity. The new orders index jumped 21 points to 23.2, while the shipments index rose 16 points to 13.1.

Unfilled orders also increased, with the index rising eight points to 14.0. Delivery times lengthened significantly, while supply availability deteriorated further, with the supply availability index falling three points to -15.1, its lowest level since June 2022. Inventories also increased.

Price pressures continued to be a concern for manufacturers. The prices paid index eased four points from last month’s four-year high to 59.5, while the prices received index rose three points to 30.6, indicating that selling price increases became more widespread.

Employment conditions remained relatively steady. The employment index held at 10.3, suggesting modest job growth, while the average workweek index came in at 9.1, pointing to an increase in hours worked.

Looking ahead, firms remained optimistic about future business conditions, although confidence moderated. The future business conditions index fell eight points to 21.0.

Manufacturers expect new orders and shipments to increase and employment to continue growing in the months ahead. However, supply availability is expected to worsen, while both future price indexes climbed further from already elevated levels, suggesting that expectations for price increases are becoming more widespread. Capital spending plans remained modest.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: US September PPI 6.3% vs 5.3% expected
item.description:
• Prior was 5.4%
  • PPI final demand m/m vs +0.5% expected
  • Prior m/m +0.4%
  • Ex-food and energy y/y vs+4.4% expected
  • Prior ex-food and energy 4.6% y/y
  • Ex-food and energy m/m vs +0.3% expected
  • Prior ex-food and energy +0.2% m/m
  • Ex-food, energy and trade y/y vs +4.7% prior
  • Ex-food, energy and trade m/m vs +0.3% prior

The Producer Price Index (PPI), published monthly by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, measures the average change in the selling prices that domestic producers receive for their output. Where the CPI tracks inflation from the consumer’s side of the register, the PPI looks at it from the seller’s side, capturing prices at the wholesale and business level before they reach households.

The headline figure is the final demand index, which BLS adopted in 2014 to replace the older finished goods measure. It covers goods, services and construction sold for personal consumption, capital investment, government and export. Services make up roughly two-thirds of the index, so it’s far more than a gauge of factory-gate prices.

Because food and energy prices swing sharply month to month, markets focus on core measures. One strips out food and energy. The narrower ex-food, energy and trade measure also removes trade services. Trade services track changes in retailer and wholesaler margins, which can be volatile and don’t always reflect underlying cost pressure.

The PPI has traditionally been watched as a pipeline indicator, on the theory that higher producer costs eventually pass through to consumers. Today its biggest market impact comes from its role in forecasting the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the core PCE price index. Several PPI components feed directly into PCE, including portfolio management fees, airfares and physician and hospital services. Economists combine the CPI and PPI releases to estimate core PCE before it’s published, so a PPI surprise in those categories can shift Fed pricing even when the headline looks benign.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morning Kickstart: Dollar retreats as yields fall, Nasdaq remains under pressure
item.description:
The U.S. dollar is lower against most of the major currencies, with the Swiss franc leading the gains. The Australian dollar is the exception after a weaker Australian jobs report.

Treasury yields are sharply lower, but that is not providing much relief for technology stocks. Nasdaq futures remain under pressure after yesterday’s sharp declines, and we have PPI, retail sales and jobless claims coming up.

In the video, I take a look at EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD, defining the bias, the risk and the targets that would give the buyers or sellers more control.

Morning Kickstart

The U.S. dollar is trading lower against most major currencies as Treasury yields retreat. However, lower yields are not translating into a broad recovery in stocks. Technology remains under pressure after yesterday’s sharp selloff, with Nasdaq futures pointing to another difficult opening.

That leaves traders with competing forces ahead of the North American session. The bond market is recovering, the dollar is softer and gold is higher, but equity traders remain cautious. PPI and retail sales will provide the next test: Are inflation pressures staying elevated, and is consumer spending holding up?

Dollar lower broadly; Australian dollar the exception

The greenback is lower against six of the seven major currencies:

  • EURUSD: 1.1212, up 0.50%.
  • GBPUSD: 1.3251, up 0.45%.
  • USDJPY: 157.90, down 0.26%.
  • USDCHF: 0.8299, down 0.56%.
  • USDCAD: 1.4200, down 0.25%.
  • NZDUSD: 0.5605, up 0.25%.
  • AUDUSD: 0.6914, down 0.79%.

The dollar’s largest decline is against the Swiss franc. Its largest gain is against the Australian dollar.

The Australian exception has a clear domestic catalyst. September employment fell 39,300, compared with expectations for a 20,000 increase, while unemployment was 4.7%. That weaker report weighed on the AUD even as the dollar declined elsewhere. investinglive.com

Currency ranges: Where are prices within the day’s trading?

EURUSD and GBPUSD are trading in the upper portions of their ranges, while USDJPY, USDCHF and USDCAD are nearer their lows. That supports the broader dollar-selling theme.

AUDUSD is at its session low, showing that sellers continue to have the stronger hand in that pair due to the weaker jobs report.

For traders, a position near an extreme matters most when the price can extend through that extreme and stay beyond it. A break that quickly fails can instead give the other side an opportunity to push back.

U.S. stocks: Nasdaq weakness continues

U.S. futures are mixed, with the Dow higher while the broader indices remain under pressure:

  • Dow futures: up 130 points.
  • S&P 500 futures: down 12.94 points.
  • Nasdaq futures: down 354 points.

Yesterday, the broader indices fell sharply, with AI and chip stocks particularly hard hit. This morning’s futures suggest that pressure has not cleared.

The overnight technology selloff also extended into Asia, where chipmakers followed Wall Street lower amid concerns over interest rates and the financing of AI investment. investinglive.com

European markets are mixed:

  • Germany’s DAX: down 0.47%.
  • France’s CAC 40: up 0.21%.
  • UK’s FTSE 100: up 0.69%.
  • Spain’s IBEX: up 0.21%.
  • Italy’s FTSE MIB: down 0.72%.

Treasury yields move sharply lower

Treasury yields are falling across the curve:

  • 2-year: 4.7488%, down 5.32 basis points.
  • 5-year: 4.9061%, down 8.59 basis points.
  • 10-year: 5.0975%, down 9.25 basis points.
  • 30-year: 5.4352%, down 8.88 basis points.

The decline in yields is an important part of the dollar’s retreat. Lower U.S. yields can reduce the relative appeal of holding dollars, although the next round of data can quickly change that calculation.

The important distinction this morning is that bonds are recovering while technology stocks remain under pressure. Lower yields alone have not been enough to bring buyers back across the broader market.

Oil edges higher; gold and silver rebound

  • WTI crude oil: $95.35, up $0.26 or 0.27%.
  • Spot gold: $4,150.85, up $46.06 or 1.12%.
  • Silver: $56.71, up approximately 1.99%.
  • Bitcoin: $80,986, down $589 or 0.72%.

Gold is recovering alongside the weaker dollar and lower Treasury yields. Bitcoin, meanwhile, remains under pressure with technology shares.

Middle East developments continue to complicate the oil outlook. InvestingLive reports persistent tensions, including Houthi attacks on Saudi targets and disruptions affecting shipping. Separately, Washington is reportedly considering easing sanctions on shadow-fleet tankers to reduce freight costs and improve Gulf oil flows. Those headlines leave traders balancing supply risks against efforts to get more oil moving. investinglive.com

A busy 8:30 AM ET data release

The North American session brings several potential catalysts together.

Producer prices:

  • Headline PPI, month over month: +0.5% expected versus +0.4% previously.
  • Headline PPI, year over year: 5.3% expected versus 5.4%.
  • PPI excluding food and energy, month over month: +0.3% expected versus +0.2%.
  • PPI excluding food and energy, year over year: 4.4% expected versus 4.6%.

The distinction between monthly and annual readings matters. Annual inflation can ease while the latest monthly increase accelerates. Traders need to look beyond the headline year-over-year number to assess whether underlying pressure is improving.

Retail sales:

  • Headline sales: +0.3% expected versus a revised +1.2% previously.
  • Sales excluding autos: +0.5% expected versus a revised +1.4%.

The prior headline reading was revised up from 1.1%, while the ex-auto reading was revised up from 1.3%.

Labor market:

  • Initial jobless claims: 200,000 expected versus 197,000.
  • Continuing claims: 1.710 million expected versus 1.716 million.

Regional manufacturing:

  • Empire State manufacturing: 10.25 expected versus 7.60.
  • Philadelphia Fed manufacturing: 28.4 expected versus 37.8.

The combination matters. Strong spending alongside firm inflation could challenge the Treasury rally. Softer spending would raise a different question about growth. The first move after the releases may reflect one report; the more lasting move will depend on how traders assess the full package.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq’s selloff may have been driven by something more concerning than just rate hike expectations
item.description:
The Nasdaq sold off sharply yesterday after US Core CPI came in higher than expected. What’s interesting, though, is that after the initial hawkish reaction, rate expectations further out the curve shifted in a dovish direction, and Treasury yields moved lower.

Copper, which is often seen as a barometer of global growth, also fell sharply following the CPI release. This might be an early sign that markets are becoming increasingly concerned about the future economic outlook.

The prolonged Middle East crisis is adding to those concerns, while persistent inflation risks could force the Fed to raise rates more than expected or keep them higher for longer. That could leave the Fed behind the curve if economic conditions start to deteriorate.

Credit spreads have been flashing warning signs for several weeks, and the equity market may now be starting to catch up. Looking ahead, the Flash PMIs, the FOMC meeting, developments in US-Iran negotiations and the US midterm elections will be key catalysts.

If economic data starts pointing to deteriorating conditions, the concerns about growth could intensify, putting further pressure on risk sentiment and the Nasdaq. On the other hand, an end to the US-Iran war could significantly change the picture by easing geopolitical uncertainty and improving the growth outlook.

item.title: Why do altcoins crash so much harder than Bitcoin?
item.description:
When you look at your screener and notice that Bitcoin is down 5%, you will more often than not also catch that smaller cryptocurrencies are plunging by 10% or even 20%. They are all part of the same crypto market, so it is natural to expect the direction of travel to be the same. But why is the magnitude of the moves so stark?

Well, the important difference is more in how these cryptocurrencies trade.

Just think of an example where you are trying to sell a second-hand Toyota Corolla. It's a fairly popular car, so chances are you'll easily find someone willing to buy it without having to knock too much your asking price.

But now, imagine that you are trying to sell a heavily customised sports car instead. Sure, the car is worth more than the Toyota Corolla and by quite a fair bit for sure. But then, how many people are actually to buy that exact car with such a niche set of specifications? Probably not very many. And if there is a sudden need to sell the car by tomorrow, you might very well have to let it go at a hefty discount in order to find someone that might be interested in buying.

So, how does this tie back to the crypto market?

With Bitcoin, there's generally a much bigger crowd of people looking to buy and sell. So even when investors start selling, there's a better chance of finding someone who would be willing to buy at a price close to the current market value.

As for smaller altcoins, it isn't quite the same story. Just imagine everyone suddenly trying to sell their heavily customised sports cars at the same time, only to realise that there aren't nearly enough interested buyers around. So, what happens next? Sellers will then have to lower their prices to attract buyers and the more desperate they become, the bigger those discounts might get.

And that is essentially what traders mean by liquidity. The easier it is to find a buyer without having to offer a hefty discount, the more liquid the market is.

Then, there's also the concept of market depth. Just imagine trying to sell an altcoin at $10, but there are only so many buyers at that price to purchase a few coins. The next set of buyers might only be willing to pay $9.50, while others are waiting at $9 to get in on the action. So if enough investors are rushing to sell, the price has to keep dropping to find willing buyers.

And if that wasn't bad enough, some traders are also betting on these cryptocurrencies using borrowed money. So when prices fall too drastically, their exchanges may automatically sell their holdings to prevent further losses. That is what we call forced liquidation. And when those automatic sales start piling up, they can push prices even lower and lead to yet another round of selling. In essence, one price drop triggers another and that turns a relatively ordinary selloff into something much more painful.

So the next time you see Bitcoin falling by 5% while your favourite altcoin tumbles by 15%, don't just assume that something terrible has happened to the smaller cryptocurrency. Sometimes, it is just simply a case of too many sellers chasing too few buyers.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US inflation worries aren't over yet as PPI and retail sales pose fresh risks for markets
item.description:
The hotter-than-expected US CPI report yesterday was already enough to give markets a bit of a headache. And despite the initial surge higher in Treasury yields fading, there's still evidence of jitters with equities staying under pressure today. So if investors are hoping for some breathing room to get by, I'm afraid there might be more bad news to deal with as we're not quite done with the inflation and economic data risks just yet.

Looking to the session ahead, there are three key US economic data releases to watch out for:

  • September PPI: This will be another inflation test, this time looking at price pressures faced by producers
  • September retail sales: This will be a key gauge of consumer spending and whether higher prices are actually slowing demand
  • Weekly initial jobless claims: This will be a timely check on whether the US labour market is starting to show more signs of weakness

Given the backdrop this week, I'd argue that the PPI and retail sales will carry the bigger risks for markets.

A hot PPI reading later will only add to inflation concerns after the stronger consumer price numbers seen yesterday. It could offer an indication that price pressures are proving to be more stubborn than the Fed would like. And if retail sales also surprises to the upside, that could stir up a potentially uncomfortable combination for the Fed to deal with.

I mean, if businesses are facing higher costs while consumers are continuing to spend freely, where exactly is the slowdown that's supposed to help bring inflation under control? On paper, that is the sort of scenario that could put renewed upward pressure on Treasury yields and the dollar, while leaving equities struggling for support - more so than they already are.

Having said that, I still reckon it's a tall order to shift Fed rate hike expectations for October at this stage. After the initial spike in market odds to the inflation numbers yesterday, Fed funds futures are now only pricing in a roughly 29% probability of a rate hike this month. That is not all too much changed from around 22% odds before the September CPI report.

As such, the market reaction to a stronger-than-expected set of numbers from both the PPI and retail sales data could arguably be something similar. It might be enough to produce a jolt upon the initial reaction, but will it be enough to really convince of a move in October? I wouldn't be one to put my money on that.

December, however, is looking almost like a done deal at this stage. So, I would argue that the data trend this week could at best solidify expectations of another move by year-end; just not for October.

The other item on the agenda today is the weekly jobless claims data. A notable rise here could complicate the picture by suggesting that the labour market is weakening even as inflation stays elevated.

So, that is pretty much the danger that markets have to navigate through today. It is not just another hot inflation number to worry about but perhaps a combination of data that could leave the Fed with even fewer options in tinkering with monetary policy.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

  • Prior +1.1%

The final figures for September are out and they're not exactly offering much comfort for the ECB. The annual readings confirm another notable jump in price pressures, adding to the inflation concerns we've been seeing across the euro area lately.

Energy prices remain the biggest culprit, surging 21.3% annually in September compared with 16.7% in August. Once again, that is largely triggered by the ongoing fallout from the Middle East conflict.

That being said, we're also starting to see broader price pressures creeping in elsewhere. Core annual inflation picked up to 1.5% from 1.1% previously, helped by a notable jump in services inflation - which rose to 2.4% from 1.9% previously. While core prices are still keeping below the 2% threshold for now, the direction of travel isn't exactly what policymakers would like to see.

For now, the ECB could still be afforded some room to be patient after having already raised interest rates twice this summer. The question now is whether the recent inflation surge warrants another move sooner rather than later. So, the central bank definitely cannot afford to be complacent either.

If higher energy prices start feeding more evidently into services and wages, then the case for another rate hike in December will only grow stronger.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Macro pulse: Treasury yields may be falling for now, but borrowing costs are still painfully high
item.description:
It's been quite a messy reaction in the bond market after the hotter-than-expected US CPI report yesterday. 10-year Treasury yields briefly pushed above 5.30% on the initial reaction before falling back now to around 5.10%, its lowest in three weeks. That's certainly a welcome change for broader markets, but it doesn't really change things all too much for the US economy.

The fact of the matter is just because borrowing costs are getting a little cheaper doesn't exactly mean that they are actually cheap.

Think about it this way. Just imagine that you're looking to buy a house and the bank offers you a mortgage at 7%. A few weeks later, that rate drops to 6.9%. Sure, that's a better situation on paper. However, does it suddenly make that dream home affordable? Probably not. And that's essentially the crux of the problem for the US economy.

10-year Treasury yields serve as a benchmark for borrowing costs across the economy. That goes from mortgage rates to corporate loans and also other forms of long-term financing. Even if these numbers don't move in lockstep with yields, they are still very much influenced by the swings in the bond market.

When yields start to move higher as they have been in the past few months, the impact of that trickles all the way down the economic ladder.

For businesses, that could mean needing to put expansion plans on hold. If financing costs are rising and eating into profits, that leaves little room to borrow millions in wanting to build a new factory or base of operations. As for households, it could mean needing to delay that home purchase or cutting back on other spending to manage existing debt.

And unless yields fall back lower to levels for businesses and households to feel comfortable again, there is no compelling reason to make different decisions to the examples above.

As such, the bigger risk for the economy isn't necessarily just Treasury yields climbing to fresh highs but how long yields will remain at these elevated levels. In other words, the economy doesn't need another surge in borrowing costs to feel the pain. Just the fact that rates are high enough for long enough i.e. "higher for longer" is already enough to do the damage.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: FX option expiries for 15 October 10am New York cut
item.description:
There are a couple of key expiry levels to take note of on the day, as highlighted in bold below.

The first is a rather chunky one for EUR/USD at the 1.1250 level, with the strike sitting just less than 40 pips away from the spot price. With the dollar retreating alongside Treasury yields as traders continue to digest the US September CPI report, that might keep this expiry level in play especially if the pair continues to nudge higher in the session ahead.

The near-term chart is also starting to turn with EUR/USD buyers breaking back above both the 100-hour and 200-hour moving averages in trading today, the first time in five weeks. That signifies a more bullish near-term picture but all eyes will be on whether Treasury yields will stick with the retreat or reverse back higher as we look to the second half of the week.

But if price action allows for EUR/USD to move closer to 1.1250, then the expiries could act as a magnet to draw price movements and keep trading action more limited around that level heading into the cut.

Then, there is one for USD/JPY at the 158.00 level - just 5 pips away from the spot price. The expiries could keep price action anchored around the figure level heading into the cut. But as mentioned, dollar pairs at the moment remain highly sensitive to moves in Treasury yields. And in the case of USD/JPY, there's also intervention headlines to be mindful of. All of that could easily outweigh the influence of option expiries.

The other expiry level worth noting is for EUR/GBP at the 0.8480 level, with the strike sitting just 11 pips above the spot price. That could attract some attention if the cross trades higher, although the impact will depend on broader euro and sterling flows for the most part.

item.title: TMGM Named Official Financial Online Trading Sponsor of BIGBANG 2026–2027 WORLD TOUR <XX : COSMOS> in Sydney
item.description:
TMGM has been named the Official Financial Online Trading Sponsor of BIGBANG 2026–2027 WORLD TOUR <XX : COSMOS> in Sydney, bringing together the Sydney-founded global broker and one of Asia’s most recognised music acts as BIGBANG celebrates its 20th anniversary.

Taking place at Accor Stadium on 31 October 2026, the Sydney concert forms part of BIGBANG’s first world tour since 2017. The tour marks two decades since the group’s debut and its return to major international stages across Asia, North America, Europe and Oceania.

The partnership marks an expansion of TMGM’s international sponsorship strategy into live entertainment. Since its founding in Sydney in 2013, TMGM has used international partnerships to build brand recognition beyond financial markets, with sport forming a significant part of its sponsorship portfolio.

Working with BIGBANG brings a new cultural dimension to that strategy. Over two decades, the South Korean group has built an international following extending across music, fashion and popular culture, creating an opportunity for TMGM to connect with audiences through one of the most established names in K-pop.
